entries.4306c47d54e9249a8281448484d3587a04f06167: <div sID="gen18708" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="17" osisID="Ezek.17" sID="Ezek.17"/> <div eID="gen18708" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18709" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen18710" type="x-p"/> God was, in the foregoing chapter, reckoning with the people of Judah, and bringing ruin upon them for their treachery in breaking covenant with him; in this chapter he is reckoning with the king of Judah for his treachery in breaking covenant with the king of Babylon; for when God came to contend with them he found many grounds of his controversy. The thing was now in doing: Zedekiah was practising with the king of Egypt underhand for assistance in a treacherous project he had formed to shake off the yoke of the king of Babylon, and violate the homage and fealty he had sworn to him. For this God by the prophet here, I. Threatens the ruin of him and his kingdom, by a parable of two eagles and a vine (<reference osisRef="Ezek.17.1-Ezek.17.10">ver. 1-10</reference>), and the explanation of that parable, <reference osisRef="Ezek.17.11-Ezek.17.21">ver. 11-21</reference>. But, in the close, II. He promises hereafter to raise the royal family of Judah again, the house of David, in the Messiah and his kingdom, <reference osisRef="Ezek.17.22-Ezek.17.24">ver. 22-24</reference>.
entries.4a27682cd5b7c8170b4faf5151f28b80cbf60891: <div eID="gen18710" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen18709" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Parable of the Eagles; The Parable Explained; Ruin of Zedekiah Predicted. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi>  593.)</title> <div sID="gen18711" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> came unto me, saying, <hi type="super">2</hi> Son of man, put forth a riddle, and speak a parable unto the house of Israel; <hi type="super">3</hi> And say, Thus saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> ; A great eagle with great wings, long-winged, full of feathers, which had divers colours, came unto Lebanon, and took the highest branch of the cedar: <hi type="super">4</hi> He cropped off the top of his young twigs, and carried it into a land of traffick; he set it in a city of merchants. <hi type="super">5</hi> He took also of the seed of the land, and planted it in a fruitful field; he placed <hi type="italic">it</hi> by great waters, <hi type="italic">and</hi> set it <hi type="italic">as</hi> a willow tree. <hi type="super">6</hi> And it grew, and became a spreading vine of low stature, whose branches turned toward him, and the roots thereof were under him: so it became a vine, and brought forth branches, and shot forth sprigs. <hi type="super">7</hi> There was also another great eagle with great wings and many feathers: and, behold, this vine did bend her roots toward him, and shot forth her branches toward him, that he might water it by the furrows of her plantation. <hi type="super">8</hi> It was planted in a good soil by great waters, that it might bring forth branches, and that it might bear fruit, that it might be a goodly vine. <hi type="super">9</hi> Say thou, Thus saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> ; Shall it prosper? shall he not pull up the roots thereof, and cut off the fruit thereof, that it wither? it shall wither in all the leaves of her spring, even without great power or many people to pluck it up by the roots thereof. <hi type="super">10</hi> Yea, behold, <hi type="italic">being</hi> planted, shall it prosper? shall it not utterly wither, when the east wind toucheth it? it shall wither in the furrows where it grew. <hi type="super">11</hi> Moreover the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> came unto me, saying, <hi type="super">12</hi> Say now to the rebellious house, Know ye not what these <hi type="italic">things mean?</hi> tell <hi type="italic">them,</hi> Behold, the king of Babylon is come to Jerusalem, and hath taken the king thereof, and the princes thereof, and led them with him to Babylon; <hi type="super">13</hi> And hath taken of the king's seed, and made a covenant with him, and hath taken an oath of him: he hath also taken the mighty of the land: <hi type="super">14</hi> That the kingdom might be base, that it might not lift itself up, <hi type="italic">but</hi> that by keeping of his covenant it might stand. <hi type="super">15</hi> But he rebelled against him in sending his ambassadors into Egypt, that they might give him horses and much people. Shall he prosper? shall he escape that doeth such <hi type="italic">things?</hi> or shall he break the covenant, and be delivered? <hi type="super">16</hi> <hi type="italic">As</hi> I live, saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> , surely in the place <hi type="italic">where</hi> the king <hi type="italic">dwelleth</hi> that made him king, whose oath he despised, and whose covenant he brake, <hi type="italic">even</hi> with him in the midst of Babylon he shall die. <hi type="super">17</hi> Neither shall Pharaoh with <hi type="italic">his</hi> mighty army and great company make for him in the war, by casting up mounts, and building forts, to cut off many persons: <hi type="super">18</hi> Seeing he despised the oath by breaking the covenant, when, lo, he had given his hand, and hath done all these <hi type="italic">things,</hi> he shall not escape. <hi type="super">19</hi> Therefore thus saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> ; <hi type="italic">As</hi> I live, surely mine oath that he hath despised, and my covenant that he hath broken, even it will I recompense upon his own head. <hi type="super">20</hi> And I will spread my net upon him, and he shall be taken in my snare, and I will bring him to Babylon, and will plead with him there for his trespass that he hath trespassed against me. <hi type="super">21</hi> And all his fugitives with all his bands shall fall by the sword, and they that remain shall be scattered toward all winds: and ye shall know that I the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> have spoken <hi type="italic">it.</hi> <div eID="gen18711" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18712" type="x-p"/> We must take all these verses together, that we may have the parable and the explanation of it at one view before us, because they will illustrate one another. 1. The prophet is appointed to <hi type="italic">put forth a riddle</hi> to the <hi type="italic">house of Israel</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.17.2">v. 2</reference>), not to puzzle them, as Samson's riddle was put forth to the Philistines, not to hide the mind of God from them in obscurity, or to leave them in uncertainty about it, one advancing one conjecture and another another, as is usual in expounding riddles; no, he is immediately to tell them the meaning of it. <hi type="italic">Let him that speaks in an unknown tongue pray that he may interpret,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.14.13">1 Cor. xiv. 13</reference>. But he must deliver this message in a riddle or parable that they might take the more notice of it, might be the more affected with it themselves, and might the better remember it and tell it to others. For these reasons God often used similitudes by his servants the prophets, and Christ himself <hi type="italic">opened his mouth in parables.</hi> Riddles and parables are used for an amusement to ourselves and an entertainment to our friends. The prophet must make use of these to see if in this dress the things of God might find acceptance, and insinuate themselves into the minds of a careless people. Note, Ministers should study to find out acceptable words, and try various methods to do good; and, as far as they have reason to think will be for edification, should both bring that which is familiar into their preaching and their preaching too into their familiar discourse, that there may not be so vast a dissimilitude as with some there is between what they say in the pulpit and what they say out. 2. He is appointed to expound this riddle to <hi type="italic">the rebellious house,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.17.12">v. 12</reference>. Though being <hi type="italic">rebellious</hi> they might justly have been left in ignorance, to see and hear and not perceive, yet the thing shall be explained to them: <hi type="italic">Know you not what these things mean?</hi> Those that knew the story, and what was now in agitation, might make a shrewd guess at the meaning of this riddle, but, that they might be left without excuse, he is to give it to them in plain terms, stripped of the metaphor. But the enigma was first propounded for them to study on awhile, and to send to their friends at Jerusalem, that they might enquire after and expect the solution of it some time after. <div eID="gen18712" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18713" type="x-p"/> Let us now see what the matter of this message is. <div eID="gen18713" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18714" type="x-p"/> I. Nebuchadnezzar had some time ago carried off Jehoiachin, the same that was called <hi type="italic">Jeconiah,</hi> when he was but eighteen years of age and had reigned in Jerusalem but <hi type="italic">three months,</hi> him and his princes and great men, and had brought them captives to Babylon, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.24.12">2 Kings xxiv. 12</reference>. This in the parable is represented by an eagle's cropping the top and tender branch of <hi type="italic">a cedar,</hi> and carrying it into <hi type="italic">a land of traffic,</hi> a <hi type="italic">city of merchants</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.17.3-Ezek.17.4">v. 3, 4</reference>), which is explained <reference osisRef="Ezek.17.12">v. 12</reference>. The <hi type="italic">king of Babylon</hi> took the <hi type="italic">king of Jerusalem,</hi> who was no more able to resist him than a young twig of a tree is to contend with the strongest bird of prey, that easily crops it off, perhaps towards the making of <hi type="italic">her nest.</hi> Nebuchadnezzar, in Daniel's vision, is <hi type="italic">a lion,</hi> the king of beasts (<reference osisRef="Dan.7.4">Dan. vii. 4</reference>); there he has <hi type="italic">eagle's wings,</hi> so swift were his motions, so speedy were his conquests. Here, in this parable, he is <hi type="italic">an eagle,</hi> the king of birds, a <hi type="italic">great eagle,</hi> that lives upon spoil and rapine, whose young ones <hi type="italic">suck up blood,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.39.30">Job xxxix. 30</reference>. His dominion extends itself far and wide, like the great and long wings of an eagle; the people are numerous, for it is <hi type="italic">full of feathers;</hi> the court is splendid, for it has <hi type="italic">divers colours,</hi> which look like <hi type="italic">embroidering,</hi> as the word is. Jerusalem is Lebanon, a forest of houses, and very pleasant. The royal family is <hi type="italic">the cedar;</hi> Jehoiachin is the <hi type="italic">top branch,</hi> the <hi type="italic">top of the young twigs,</hi> which he crops off. Babylon is the <hi type="italic">land of traffic</hi> and <hi type="italic">city of merchants</hi> where it is set. And the king of Judah, being of the house of David, will think himself much degraded and disgraced to be lodged among tradesmen; but he must make the best of it. <div eID="gen18714" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18715" type="x-p"/> II. When he carried him to Babylon he made his uncle Zedekiah king in his room, <reference osisRef="Ezek.17.5-Ezek.17.6">v. 5, 6</reference>. His name was <hi type="italic">Mattaniah—the gift of the Lord,</hi> which Nebuchadnezzar changed into <hi type="italic">Zedekiah—the justice of the Lord,</hi> to remind him to be just like the God he called his, for fear of his justice. This was <hi type="italic">one of the seed of the land,</hi> a native, not a foreigner, not one of his Babylonian princes; he was <hi type="italic">planted in a fruitful field,</hi> for so Jerusalem as yet was; he <hi type="italic">placed it by great waters,</hi> where it would be likely to grow, like <hi type="italic">a willow-tree,</hi> which grows quickly, and grows best in moist ground, but is never designed nor expected to be a stately tree. He <hi type="italic">set it with</hi> care and <hi type="italic">circumspection</hi> (so some read it); he wisely provided that it might grow, but that it might not grow too big. <hi type="italic">He took of the king's seed</hi> (so it is explained, <reference osisRef="Ezek.17.13">v. 13</reference>) and <hi type="italic">made a covenant with him</hi> that he should have the kingdom, and enjoy the regal power and dignity, provided he held it as his vassal, dependent on him and accountable to him. He <hi type="italic">took an oath of him,</hi> made him swear allegiance to him, swear by his own God, the God of Israel, that he would be a faithful tributary to him, <reference osisRef="2Chr.36.13">2 Chron. xxxvi. 13</reference>. He also <hi type="italic">took away the mighty of the land,</hi> the chief of the men of war, partly as hostages for the performance of the covenant, and partly that, the land being thereby weakened, the king might be the less able, and therefore the less in temptation, to break his league. What he designed we are told (<reference osisRef="Ezek.17.14">v. 14</reference>): <hi type="italic">That the kingdom might be base,</hi> in respect both of honour and strength, might neither be a rival with its powerful neighbours, nor a terror to its feeble ones, as it had been, that <hi type="italic">it might not left up itself</hi> to vie with the kingdom of Babylon, or to bear down any of the petty states that were in subjection to it. But yet he designed that by <hi type="italic">the keeping of this covenant it might stand,</hi> and continue a kingdom. Hereby the pride and ambition of that haughty potentate would be gratified, who aimed to be <hi type="italic">like the Most High</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.14.14">Isa. xiv. 14</reference>), to have all about him subject to him. Now see here, 1. How sad a change sin made with the royal family of Judah. Time was when all the nations about were tributaries to that; now that has not only lost its dominion over other nations, but has itself become a tributary. <hi type="italic">How has the gold become dim!</hi> Nations by sin sell their liberty, and princes their dignity, and <hi type="italic">profane their crowns by casting them to the ground.</hi> 2. How wisely Zedekiah did for himself in accepting these terms, though they were dishonourable, when necessity brought him to it. A man may live very comfortably and contentedly, though he cannot bear a part, and make a figure, as formerly. A kingdom may stand firmly and safely, though it do not stand so high as it has sometimes done; and so may a family. <div eID="gen18715" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18716" type="x-p"/> III. Zedekiah, while he continued faithful to the king of Babylon, did very well, and, if he would but have reformed his kingdom, and returned to God and his duty, he would have done better, and by that means might soon have recovered his former dignity, <reference osisRef="Ezek.17.6">v. 6</reference>. This plant grew, and though it was <hi type="italic">set as a willow-tree,</hi> and little account was made of it, yet it became <hi type="italic">a spreading vine of low stature,</hi> a great blessing to his own country, and his fruits <hi type="italic">made glad their hearts;</hi> and it is better to be a spreading vine of low stature than a lofty cedar of no use. Nebuchadnezzar was pleased, for <hi type="italic">the branches turned towards him,</hi> and rested on him as the vine on the wall, and he had his share of the fruits of this vine; <hi type="italic">the roots thereof</hi> too were <hi type="italic">under him,</hi> and at his disposal. The Jews had reason to be pleased, for they sat under their own vine, which <hi type="italic">brought forth branches, and shot forth sprigs,</hi> and looked pleasant and promising. See how gradually the judgments of God came upon this provoking people, how God gave them respite and so gave them space to repent. He made <hi type="italic">their kingdom base,</hi> to try if that would humble them, before he made it no kingdom; yet left it easy for them, to try if that would win upon them to return to him, that the troubles threatened might be prevented. <div eID="gen18716" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18717" type="x-p"/> IV. Zedekiah knew not when he was well off, but grew impatient of the disgrace of being a tributary to the king of Babylon, and, to get clear of it, entered into a private league with the king of Egypt. He had no reason to complain that the king of Babylon put any new hardships upon him or improved his advantages against him, that he oppressed or impoverished his country, for, as the prophet had said before (<reference osisRef="Ezek.17.6">v. 6</reference>) to aggravate his treachery, he shows again (<reference osisRef="Ezek.17.8">v. 8</reference>) what a fair way he was in to be considerable: <hi type="italic">He was planted in a good soil by great waters;</hi> his family was likely enough to be built up, and his exchequer to be filled, in a little time, so that, if he had dealt faithfully, he might have been <hi type="italic">a goodly vine.</hi> But there was <hi type="italic">another great eagle</hi> that he had an affection for, and put a confidence in, and that was the <hi type="italic">king of Egypt,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.17.7">v. 7</reference>. Those two great potentates, the kings of Babylon and Egypt, were but two great eagles, <hi type="italic">birds of prey.</hi> This great eagle of Egypt is said to have <hi type="italic">great wings,</hi> but not to be <hi type="italic">long-winged</hi> as the king of Babylon, because, though the kingdom of Egypt was strong, yet it was not of such a vast extent as that of Babylon was. The great eagle is said to have <hi type="italic">many feathers,</hi> much wealth and many soldiers, which he depended upon as a substantial defence, but which really were no more than so <hi type="italic">may feathers.</hi> Zedekiah, promising himself liberty, made himself a vassal to the king of Egypt, foolishly expecting ease by changing his master. Now <hi type="italic">this vine</hi> did secretly and under-hand <hi type="italic">bend her roots towards</hi> the king of Egypt, that great eagle, and after awhile did openly <hi type="italic">shoot forth her branches towards him,</hi> give him an intimation how much she coveted an alliance with him, <hi type="italic">that he might water it by the furrows of her plantation,</hi> whereas it was <hi type="italic">planted by great waters,</hi> and did not need any assistance from him. This is expounded, <reference osisRef="Ezek.17.15">v. 15</reference>. Zedekiah rebelled against the king of Babylon in <hi type="italic">sending his ambassadors into Egypt,</hi> that they might <hi type="italic">give him horses and much people,</hi> to enable him to contend with the king of Babylon. See what a change sin had made with the people of God! God promised that they should be a numerous people, as the sand of the sea; yet now, if their king had occasion for <hi type="italic">much people,</hi> he must send to Egypt for them, they being for sin <hi type="italic">diminished and brought low,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.107.39">Ps. cvii. 39</reference>. See also the folly of fretful discontented spirits, that ruin themselves by striving to better themselves, whereas they might be easy and happy enough if they would but <hi type="italic">make the best of that which is.</hi> <div eID="gen18717" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18718" type="x-p"/> V. God here threatens Zedekiah with the utter destruction of him and his kingdom, and, in displeasure against him, passes that doom upon him for his treacherous revolt from the king of Babylon. This is represented in the parable (<reference osisRef="Ezek.17.9">v. 9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.17.19">19</reference>) by the <hi type="italic">plucking up of this vine by the roots, the cutting off of the fruit,</hi> and <hi type="italic">the withering of the leaves,</hi> the leaves <hi type="italic">of her spring,</hi> when they are in their greenness (<reference osisRef="Job.8.12">Job viii. 12</reference>), before they begin in autumn to wither of themselves. The project shall be blasted; it shall <hi type="italic">utterly wither.</hi> The affairs of this perfidious prince shall be ruined past retrieve; as a vine when the east wind blasts it, so that it shall be fit for nothing but the fire (as we had it in that parable, <reference osisRef="Ezek.15.4">ch. xv. 4</reference>), it shall wither even <hi type="italic">in the furrows where it grew,</hi> though they were ever so well watered. It shall be destroyed <hi type="italic">without great power or many people to pluck it up;</hi> for what need is there of raising the militia to pluck up a vine? Note, God can bring great things to pass without much ado. He needs not great power and many people to effect his purposes; a handful will serve if he pleases. He can without any difficulty ruin a sinful king and kingdom, and make no more of it than we do of rooting up a tree that cumbers the ground. In the explanation of the parable the sentence is very largely recorded: <hi type="italic">Shall he prosper?</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.17.15">v. 15</reference>. Can he expect to do ill and fare well? Nay, shall he that does such wicked things <hi type="italic">escape?</hi> Shall he <hi type="italic">break the covenant, and be delivered</hi> from that vengeance which is the just punishment of his treachery? No; can he expect to do ill and not suffer ill? Let him hear his doom. <div eID="gen18718" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18719" type="x-p"/> 1. It is ratified by the oath of God (<reference osisRef="Ezek.17.16">v. 16</reference>): <hi type="italic">As I live, saith the Lord God, he shall die</hi> for it. This intimates how highly God resented the crime, and how sure and severe the punishment of it would be. God <hi type="italic">swears in his wrath,</hi> as he did <reference osisRef="Ps.95.11">Ps. xcv. 11</reference>. Note, As God's promises are confirmed with an oath, for comfort to the saints, so are his threatenings, for terror to the wicked. As sure as God lives and is happy (I may add, and as long), so sure, so long, shall impenitent sinners die and be miserable. <div eID="gen18719" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18720" type="x-p"/> 2. It is justified by the heinousness of the crime he had been guilty of. (1.) He had been very ungrateful to his benefactor, who had <hi type="italic">made him king,</hi> and undertook to protect him, had made him a prince when he might as easily have made him a prisoner. Note, It is a sin against God to be unkind to our friends and to lift up the heel against those that have helped to raise us. (2.) He had been very false to him whom he had covenanted with. This is mostly insisted on: He <hi type="italic">despised the oath.</hi> When his conscience or friends reminded him of it he made a jest of it, put on a daring resolution, and <hi type="italic">broke it,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.17.15-Ezek.17.16">v. 15, 16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.17.18">18</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.17.19">19</reference>. He broke through it, and took a pride in making nothing of it, as a great tyrant in our own day, whose maxim (they say) it is, <hi type="italic">That princes ought not to be slaves to their word any further than it is for their interest.</hi> That which aggravated Zedekiah's perfidiousness was that the oath by which he had bound himself to the king of Babylon was, [1.] A solemn oath. An emphasis is laid upon this (<reference osisRef="Ezek.17.18">v. 18</reference>): <hi type="italic">When, lo, he had given his hand,</hi> as a confederate with the king of Babylon, not only as his subject, but as his friend, the joining of hands being a token of the joining of hearts. [2.] As sacred oath. God says (<reference osisRef="Ezek.17.19">v. 19</reference>): It is <hi type="italic">my oath</hi> that he has despised and <hi type="italic">my covenant that he has broken.</hi> In every solemn oath God is appealed to as a witness of the sincerity of him that swears, and invocated as a judge and revenger of his treachery if he now swear falsely or at any time hereafter break his oath. But the oath of allegiance to a prince is particularly called <hi type="italic">the oath of God</hi> (<reference osisRef="Eccl.8.2">Eccl. viii. 2</reference>), as if that had something in it more sacred than another oath; for princes are <hi type="italic">ministers of God to us for good,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.13.4">Rom. xiii. 4</reference>. Now Zedekiah's breaking this oath and covenant is the sin which God will <hi type="italic">recompense upon his own head</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.17.19">v. 19</reference>), the <hi type="italic">trespass which he has trespassed against God,</hi> for which God will <hi type="italic">plead with him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.17.20">v. 20</reference>. Note, Perjury is a heinous sin and highly provoking to the God of heaven. It would not serve for an excuse, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> That he who took this oath was a king, a king of the house of David, whose liberty and dignity might surely set him above the obligation of oaths. No; though kings are gods to us, they are men to God, and not exempt from his law and judgment. The prince is doubtless as firmly bound before God to the people by his coronation-oath as the people are to the princes by the oath of allegiance. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Nor that this oath was sworn to the king of Babylon, a heathen prince, worse than a heretic, with whom the church of Rome says, <hi type="italic">No faith is to be kept.</hi> No; though Nebuchadnezzar was a worshipper of false gods, yet the true God will avenge this quarrel when one of his worshippers breaks his league with him; for truth is a debt due to all men; and, if the professors of the true religion deal perfidiously with those of a false religion, their profession will be so far from excusing, much less justifying them, that it aggravates their sin, and God will the more surely and severely punish it, because by it they give occasion to the enemies of the Lord to blaspheme; as that Mahometan prince, who, when the Christians broke their league with him, cried out, <hi type="italic">O Jesus! are these thy Christians? Thirdly,</hi> Nor would it justify him that the oath was extorted from him by a conqueror, for the covenant was made upon a valuable consideration. He held his life and crown upon this condition, that he should be faithful and bear true allegiance to the king of Babylon; and, if he enjoy the benefit of his bargain, it is very unjust if he do not observe the terms. Let him know then that, having <hi type="italic">despised the oath,</hi> and <hi type="italic">broken the covenant,</hi> he <hi type="italic">shall not escape.</hi> And if the contempt and violation of such an oath, such a covenant as this, would be so punished, of how much sorer punishment shall those be thought worthy who break covenant with God (when, <hi type="italic">lo, they had given their hand</hi> upon it that they would be faithful), who <hi type="italic">tread under foot the blood</hi> of that <hi type="italic">covenant</hi> as an unholy thing? Between the covenants there is no comparison. <div eID="gen18720" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18721" type="x-p"/> 3. It is particularized in divers instances, wherein the punishment is made to answer the sin. (1.) He had rebelled against the king of Babylon, and the king of Babylon should be his effectual conqueror. In the place where that king <hi type="italic">dwells</hi> whose <hi type="italic">covenant he broke,</hi> even <hi type="italic">with him in the midst of Babylon he shall die,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.17.16">v. 16</reference>. He thinks to get out of his hands, but he shall fall, more than before, into his hands. God himself will now take part with the king of Babylon against him: <hi type="italic">I will spread my net upon him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.17.20">v. 20</reference>. God has a net for those who deal perfidiously and think to escape his righteous judgments, in which those shall be taken and held who would not be held by the bond of an oath and covenant. Zedekiah dreaded Babylon: "Thither I will bring him," says God, "and <hi type="italic">plead with him there.</hi>" Men will justly be forced upon that calamity which they endeavour by sin to flee from. (2.) He had <hi type="italic">relied upon the king of Egypt,</hi> and the king of Egypt should be his ineffectual helper: <hi type="italic">Pharaoh with his mighty army shall not make for him in the war</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.17.17">v. 17</reference>), shall to him no service, nor give any check to the progress of the Chaldean forces; he shall not assist him in the <hi type="italic">siege</hi> by <hi type="italic">casting up mounts and building forts,</hi> nor in battle by <hi type="italic">cutting off many person.</hi> Note, Every creature is that to us which God makes it to be; and he commonly weakens and withers that <hi type="italic">arm of flesh</hi> which we trust in and stay ourselves upon. Now was again fulfilled what was spoken on a former similar occasion (<reference osisRef="Isa.30.7">Isa. xxx. 7</reference>), <hi type="italic">The Egyptians shall help in vain.</hi> They did so; for though, upon the approach of the Egyptian army, the Chaldeans withdrew from the siege of Jerusalem, upon their retreat they returned to it again and took it. It should seem, the Egyptians were not hearty, had strength enough, but no good-will, to help Zedekiah. Note, Those who deal treacherously with those who put a confidence in them will justly be dealt treacherously with by those they put a confidence in. Yet the Egyptians were not the only states Zedekiah stayed himself upon; he had bands of his own to stand by him, but those bands, though we may suppose they were veteran troops and the best soldiers his kingdom afforded, shall become <hi type="italic">fugitives,</hi> shall quit their posts, and make the best of their way, and shall <hi type="italic">fall by the sword</hi> of the enemy, and the <hi type="italic">remains of them shall be scattered,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.17.21">v. 21</reference>. This was fulfilled <hi type="italic">when the city was broken up and all the men of war fled,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.52.7">Jer. lii. 7</reference>. Then <hi type="italic">you shall know that I the Lord have spoken it.</hi> Note, Sooner or later God's word will prove itself; and those who will not believe shall find by experience the reality and weight of it.
entries.fb3372b1144bea9ef56b67acb638cf52f69a1d18: <div eID="gen18721" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Promises of Mercy. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 593.)</title> <div sID="gen18722" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">22</hi> Thus saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> ; I will also take of the highest branch of the high cedar, and will set <hi type="italic">it;</hi> I will crop off from the top of his young twigs a tender one, and will plant <hi type="italic">it</hi> upon a high mountain and eminent: <hi type="super">23</hi> In the mountain of the height of Israel will I plant it: and it shall bring forth boughs, and bear fruit, and be a goodly cedar: and under it shall dwell all fowl of every wing; in the shadow of the branches thereof shall they dwell. <hi type="super">24</hi> And all the trees of the field shall know that I the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> have brought down the high tree, have exalted the low tree, have dried up the green tree, and have made the dry tree to flourish: I the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> have spoken and have done <hi type="italic">it.</hi> <div eID="gen18722" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18723" type="x-p"/> When the royal family of Judah was brought to desolation by the captivity of Jehoiachin and Zedekiah it might be asked, "What has now become of the covenant of royalty made with David, that <hi type="italic">his children should sit upon his throne for evermore?</hi> Do the <hi type="italic">sure mercies of David</hi> prove thus unsure?" To this it is sufficient for the silencing of the objectors to answer that the promise was conditional. If <hi type="italic">they will keep my covenant,</hi> then they shall continue, <reference osisRef="Ps.132.12">Ps. cxxxii. 12</reference>. But David's posterity broke the condition, and so forfeited the promise. But the unbelief of man shall not invalidate the promise of God. He will find out another <hi type="italic">seed of David</hi> in which it shall be accomplished; and that is promised in these verses. <div eID="gen18723" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18724" type="x-p"/> I. The house of David shall again be magnified, and out of its ashes another phoenix shall arise. The metaphor of a tree, which was made us of in the threatening, is here presented in the promise, <reference osisRef="Ezek.17.22-Ezek.17.23">v. 22, 23</reference>. This promise had its accomplishment in part when Zerubbabel, a branch of the house of David, was raised up to head the Jews in their return out of captivity, and to rebuild the city and temple and re-establish their church and state; but it was to have its full accomplishment in the kingdom of the Messiah, who was a root out of a dry ground, and to whom God, according to promise, gave <hi type="italic">the throne of his father David,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.1.32">Luke i. 32</reference>. 1. God himself undertakes the reviving and restoring of the house of David. Nebuchadnezzar was the <hi type="italic">great eagle</hi> that had attempted the re-establishing of the house of David in a dependence upon him, <reference osisRef="Ezek.17.5">v. 5</reference>. But the attempt miscarried; his plantation withered and was plucked up. "Well," says God, "the next shall be of my planting: <hi type="italic">I will also take of the highest branch of the high cedar and I will set it.</hi>" Note, As men have their designs, God also has his designs; but his will prosper when theirs are blasted. Nebuchadnezzar prided himself in setting up kingdoms at his pleasure, <reference osisRef="Dan.5.19">Dan. v. 19</reference>. But those kingdoms soon had an end, whereas the <hi type="italic">God of heaven sets up a kingdom that shall never be destroyed,</hi> <reference osisRef="Dan.2.44">Dan. ii. 44</reference>. 2. The house of David is revived in a <hi type="italic">tender one cropped from the top of his young twigs.</hi> Zerubbabel was so; that which was hopeful in him was but the <hi type="italic">day of small things</hi> (<reference osisRef="Zech.4.10">Zech. iv. 10</reference>), yet before him <hi type="italic">great mountains</hi> were <hi type="italic">made plain.</hi> Our Lord Jesus was <hi type="italic">the highest branch of the high cedar,</hi> the furthest of all from <hi type="italic">the root</hi> (for soon after he appeared the <hi type="italic">house of David</hi> was all cut off and extinguished), but the nearest of all to heaven, for his kingdom was not of this world. He was <hi type="italic">taken from the top of the young twigs,</hi> for he is <hi type="italic">the man, the branch, a tender</hi> plant, and a <hi type="italic">root out of a dry ground</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.53.2">Isa. liii. 2</reference>), but a <hi type="italic">branch of righteousness, the planting of the Lord, that he may be glorified.</hi> 3. This branch is planted <hi type="italic">in a high mountain</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.17.22">v. 22</reference>), in the <hi type="italic">mountain of the height of Israel,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.17.23">v. 23</reference>. Thither he brought Zerubbabel in triumph; there he raised up his son Jesus, sent him to gather the <hi type="italic">lost sheep of the house of Israel</hi> that were <hi type="italic">scattered upon the mountains,</hi> set him <hi type="italic">his king</hi> upon <hi type="italic">his holy hill of Zion,</hi> sent forth the gospel from <hi type="italic">Mount Zion, the word of the Lord from Jerusalem;</hi> there, in the <hi type="italic">height of Israel,</hi> a nation which all its neighbours had an eye upon as conspicuous and illustrious, was the Christian church first planted. The churches of Judea were the most primitive churches. The unbelieving Jews did what they could to prevent its being planted there; but who can pluck up what God will plant? 4. Thence it spreads far and wide. The Jewish state, though it began very low in Zerubbabel's time, was set as a tender branch, which might easily be plucked up, yet took root, spread strangely, and after some time became very considerable; those of other nations, <hi type="italic">fowl of every wing,</hi> put themselves under the protection of it. The Christian church was at first like a grain of mustard-seed, but became, like this tender branch, a great tree, its beginning small, but its latter end increasing to admiration. When the Gentiles flocked into the church then did the <hi type="italic">fowl of every wing</hi> (even the birds of prey, which those preyed upon, as the <hi type="italic">wolf and the lamb</hi> feeding together, <reference osisRef="Isa.11.6">Isa. xi. 6</reference>) come and <hi type="italic">dwell under the shadow of this goodly cedar.</hi> See <reference osisRef="Dan.4.21">Dan. iv. 21</reference>. <div eID="gen18724" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18725" type="x-p"/> II. God himself will herein be glorified, <reference osisRef="Ezek.17.24">v. 24</reference>. The setting up of the Messiah's kingdom in the world shall discover more clearly than ever to the children of men that <hi type="italic">God is the King of all the earth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.47.7">Ps. xlvii. 7</reference>. Never was there a more full conviction given of this truth, that all things are governed by an infinitely wise and mighty Providence, than that which was given by the exaltation of Christ and the establishment of his kingdom among men; for by that it appeared that God has all hearts in his hand, and the sovereign disposal of all affairs. <hi type="italic">All the trees of the field shall know,</hi> 1. That the tree which God will have to be <hi type="italic">brought down,</hi> and <hi type="italic">dried up,</hi> shall be so, though it be ever so high and stately, ever so green and flourishing. Neither honour nor wealth, neither external advancements nor internal endowments, will secure men from humbling withering providence. 2. That the tree which God will have to be exalted, and to flourish, shall so be, shall so do, though ever so low, and ever so dry. The house of Nebuchadnezzar, that now makes so great a figure, shall be extirpated, and the house of David, that now makes so mean a figure, shall become famous again; and the Jewish nation, that is now despicable, shall be considerable. The kingdom of Satan, that has borne so long, so large, a sway, shall be broken, and the kingdom of Christ, that was looked upon with contempt, shall be established. The Jews, who, in respect of church-privileges, had been high and green, shall be thrown out, and the Gentiles, who had been low and dry trees, shall be taken in their room, <reference osisRef="Isa.54.1">Isa. liv. 1</reference>. All the enemies of Christ shall be abased and made his footstool, and his interests shall be confirmed and advanced: <hi type="italic">I the Lord have spoken</hi> (it is the decree, the declared decree, that Christ must be exalted, must be the headstone of the corner), and <hi type="italic">I have done it,</hi> that is, I will do it in due time, but it is as sure to be done as if it were done already. With men <hi type="italic">saying and doing are two things,</hi> but they are not so with God. What he has spoken we may be sure that he will do, nor shall one iota or tittle of his word fall to the ground, for <hi type="italic">he is not a man, that he should lie, or the son of man, that he should repent</hi> either of his threatenings or of his promises.  <chapter eID="Ezek.17"/> <div eID="gen18725" type="x-p"/>

entries.4470b5f88fc12c34923d79160489db4e54ab99c2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11264"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 17</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ezek.17.1-Ezek.17.24">Eze 17:1-24</reference>. Parable of the Two Great Eagles, and the Cropping of the Cedar of Lebanon. Judah Is to Be Judged for Revolting from Babylon, Which Had Set Up Zedekiah instead of Jehoiachin, to Egypt; God Himself, as the Rival of the Babylonian King, Is to Plant the Gospel Cedar of Messiah.</title> <div sID="gen20343" type="x-p"/> The date of the prophecy is between the sixth month of Zedekiah's sixth year of reign and the fifth month of the seventh year after the carrying away of Jehoiachin, that is, five years before the destruction of Jerusalem [Henderson].<div eID="gen20343" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20344" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11264"/><hi type="bold">2. riddle--</hi>a continued allegory, expressed enigmatically, requiring more than common acumen and serious thought. The Hebrew is derived from a root, "sharp," that is, calculated to stimulate attention and whet the intellect. Distinct from "fable," in that it teaches not fiction, but fact. Not like the ordinary riddle, designed to puzzle, but to instruct. The "riddle" is here identical with the "parable," only that the former refers to the obscurity, the latter to the likeness of the figure to the thing compared. <div eID="gen20344" type="x-p"/>
entries.f4c327442f2c74f964ccd16fe2901a11c84e80a9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11265"/><div sID="gen20345" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11265"/><hi type="bold">3. eagle--</hi>the king of birds. The literal Hebrew is, "the great eagle." The symbol of the Assyrian supreme god, Nisroch; so applied to "the great king" of Babylon, his vicegerent on earth (<reference osisRef="Jer.48.40">Jr 48:40</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.49.22">49:22</reference>). His "wings" are his great forces. Such symbols were familiar to the Jews, who saw them portrayed on the great buildings of Babylon; such as are now seen in the Assyrian remains.<div eID="gen20345" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20346" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">long-winged--</hi>implying the wide extent of his empire.<div eID="gen20346" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20347" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">full of feathers--</hi>when they have been renewed after moulting; and so in the full freshness of renovated youth (<reference osisRef="Ps.103.5">Psa 103:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.40.31">Is 40:31</reference>). Answering to the many peoples which, as tributaries, constituted the strength of Babylon.<div eID="gen20347" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20348" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">divers colours--</hi>the golden eagle, marked with star-like spots, supposed to be the largest of eagles [Bochart]. Answering to the variety of languages, habits, and costumes of the peoples subject to Babylon.<div eID="gen20348" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20349" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">came unto Lebanon--</hi>continuing the metaphor: as the eagle frequents mountains, not cities. The temple at Jerusalem was called "Lebanon" by the Jews [Eusebius], because its woodwork was wholly of cedars of Lebanon. "The mountain of the Lord's house" (<reference osisRef="Isa.2.2">Is 2:2</reference>). Jerusalem, however, is chiefly meant, the chief seat of civil honor, as Lebanon was of external elevation.<div eID="gen20349" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20350" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">took the highest branch--</hi>King Jeconiah, then but eighteen years old, and many of the chiefs and people with him (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.24.8">2Ki 24:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.24.12-2Kgs.24.16">12-16</reference>). The Hebrew for "highest branch" is, properly, the fleece-like tuft at the top of the tree. (So in <reference osisRef="Ezek.31.3-Ezek.31.14">Eze 31:3-14</reference>). The cedar, as a tall tree, is the symbol of kingly elevation (compare <reference osisRef="Dan.4.10-Dan.4.12">Da 4:10-12</reference>). <div eID="gen20350" type="x-p"/>
entries.6ef60d917e14ccf9c85d085a2299488797c15cdc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11266"/><div sID="gen20351" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11266"/><hi type="bold">4. land of traffic ... merchants--</hi>Babylon (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.24.15">2Ki 24:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.24.16">16</reference>), famous for its transport traffic on the Tigris and Euphrates. Also, by its connection with the Persian Gulf, it carried on much commerce with India. <div eID="gen20351" type="x-p"/>
entries.23ffc3291d7166ec1abaf8987b365cc9ee12cc00: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11267"/><div sID="gen20352" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11267"/><hi type="bold">5. seed of the land--</hi>not a foreign production, but one native in the region; a son of the soil, not a foreigner: Zedekiah, uncle of Jehoiachin, of David's family.<div eID="gen20352" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20353" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in a fruitful field--</hi>literally, a "field of seed"; that is, fit for propagating and continuing the seed of the royal family.<div eID="gen20353" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20354" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as a willow--</hi>derived from a Hebrew root, "to overflow," from its fondness for water (<reference osisRef="Isa.44.4">Is 44:4</reference>). Judea was "a land of brooks of water and fountains" (<reference osisRef="Deut.8.7-Deut.8.9">De 8:7-9</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="John.3.23">Joh 3:23</reference>). <div eID="gen20354" type="x-p"/>
entries.d45d70c7d973c85472970180ac8672a24237d4cd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11268"/><div sID="gen20355" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11268"/><hi type="bold">6. vine of low stature--</hi>not now, as before, a stately "cedar"; the kingdom of Judah was to be prosperous, but not elevated.<div eID="gen20355" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20356" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">branches turned toward him--</hi>expressing the fealty of Zedekiah as a vassal looking up to Nebuchadnezzar, to whom Judah owed its peace and very existence as a separate state. The "branches" mean his sons and the other princes and nobles.<div eID="gen20356" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20357" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">The roots ... under him--</hi>The stability of Judah depended on Babylon. The repetition "branches" and "springs" is in order to mark the ingratitude of Zedekiah, who, not content with moderate prosperity, revolted from him to whom he had sworn allegiance. <div eID="gen20357" type="x-p"/>
entries.92c89405abf17ebba60adb6eb33b3449ed452e18: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11269"/><div sID="gen20358" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11269"/><hi type="bold">7. another ... eagle--</hi>the king of Egypt (<reference osisRef="Ezek.17.15">Eze 17:15</reference>). The "long-winged" of <reference osisRef="Ezek.17.3">Eze 17:3</reference> is omitted, as Egypt had not such a wide empire and large armies as Babylon.<div eID="gen20358" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20359" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">vine ... bend ... roots towards him--</hi>literally, "thirsted after him with its roots"; expressing the longings after Egypt in the Jewish heart. Zedekiah sought the alliance of Egypt, as though by it he could throw off his dependence on Babylon (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.24.7">2Ki 24:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.24.20">20</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.36.13">2Ch 36:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.37.5">Jr 37:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.37.7">7</reference>).<div eID="gen20359" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20360" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">water it by ... furrows of ... plantation--</hi>that is, in the garden beds (Judea) wherein (the vine) it was planted. Rather, "by" or "out of the furrows." It refers to the waters of Egypt, the Nile being made to water the fields by means of small canals or "furrows"; these waters are the figure of the auxiliary forces wherewith Egypt tried to help Judah. See the same figure, <reference osisRef="Isa.8.7">Is 8:7</reference>. But see on <reference osisRef="Ezek.17.10">Eze 17:10</reference>, "furrows where it grew." <div eID="gen20360" type="x-p"/>
entries.ef58f90e1ee3f2cdd926e121f275bc7ef051b4f6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11270"/><div sID="gen20361" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11270"/><hi type="bold">8. It was planted in a good soil--</hi>It was not want of the necessaries of life, nor oppression on the port of Nebuchadnezzar, which caused Zedekiah to revolt: it was gratuitous ambition, pride, and ingratitude. <div eID="gen20361" type="x-p"/>
entries.491b805e1d4d21cdd1bc9f1aab1e74bc89acf1f9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11271"/><div sID="gen20362" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11271"/><hi type="bold">9. Shall it prosper?--</hi>Could it be that gratuitous treason should prosper? God will not allow it. "It," that is, the vine.<div eID="gen20362" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20363" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he ... pull up--</hi>that is, the first eagle, or Nebuchadnezzar.<div eID="gen20363" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20364" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in all ... leaves of her spring--</hi>that is, all its springing (sprouting) leaves.<div eID="gen20364" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20365" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">without great power or many--</hi>It shall not need all the forces of Babylon to destroy it; a small division of the army will suffice because God will deliver it into Nebuchadnezzar's hand (<reference osisRef="Jer.37.10">Jr 37:10</reference>). <div eID="gen20365" type="x-p"/>
entries.e4e711211055eed9a4754e17839183983a5e935a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11272"/><div sID="gen20366" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11272"/><hi type="bold">10. being planted--</hi>that is, "though planted."<div eID="gen20366" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20367" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">east wind--</hi>The east wind was noxious to vegetation in Palestine; a fit emblem of Babylon, which came from the northeast.<div eID="gen20367" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20368" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wither in ... furrows where it grew--</hi>Zedekiah was taken at Jericho, on Jewish soil (<reference osisRef="Jer.52.8">Jr 52:8</reference>). "It shall wither, although it has furrows from which it expects continual waterings" [Calvin], (<reference osisRef="Ezek.19.12">Eze 19:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.13.15">Ho 13:15</reference>). <div eID="gen20368" type="x-p"/>
entries.c3105718c91046f2800427573ca58351ee7fe58c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11273"/><div sID="gen20369" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11273"/><hi type="bold">12. Know ye not--</hi>He upbraided them with moral, leading to intellectual, stupidity.<div eID="gen20369" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20370" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">hath taken the king--</hi>Jeconiah or Jehoiachin (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.24.11">2Ki 24:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.24.12-2Kgs.24.16">12-16</reference>). <div eID="gen20370" type="x-p"/>
entries.89ec4685ebbe17df0c5219449880f3a6c1cf28b2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11274"/><div sID="gen20371" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11274"/><hi type="bold">13. the king's seed--</hi>Zedekiah, Jeconiah's uncle.<div eID="gen20371" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20372" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">taken ... oath of him--</hi>swearing fealty as a vassal to Nebuchadnezzar (<reference osisRef="2Chr.36.13">2Ch 36:13</reference>).<div eID="gen20372" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20373" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">also taken the mighty--</hi>as hostages for the fulfilment of the covenant; whom, therefore, Zedekiah exposed to death by his treason. <div eID="gen20373" type="x-p"/>
entries.9fd362cbdfb92c17e866185e091f322758510617: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11275"/><div sID="gen20374" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11275"/><hi type="bold">14. That the kingdom might be base--</hi>that is, low as to national elevation by being Nebuchadnezzar's dependent; but, at the same time, safe and prosperous, if faithful to the "oath." Nebuchadnezzar dealt sincerely and openly in proposing conditions, and these moderate ones; therefore Zedekiah's treachery was the baser and was a counterpart to their treachery towards God. <div eID="gen20374" type="x-p"/>
entries.c388e17c68b0c807f9f379141b562aa14832ea4e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11276"/><div sID="gen20375" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11276"/><hi type="bold">15. he rebelled--</hi>God permitted this because of His wrath against Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.24.20">2Ki 24:20</reference>).<div eID="gen20375" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20376" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">horses--</hi>in which Egypt abounded and which were forbidden to Israel to seek from Egypt, or indeed to "multiply" at all (<reference osisRef="Deut.17.16">De 17:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.31.1">Is 31:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.31.3">3</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Isa.36.9">Is 36:9</reference>). Diodorus Siculus [1.45] says that the whole region from Thebes to Memphis was filled with royal stalls, so that twenty thousand chariots with two horses in each could be furnished for war.<div eID="gen20376" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20377" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Shall he prosper?--</hi>The third time this question is asked, with an indignant denial understood (<reference osisRef="Ezek.17.9">Eze 17:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.17.10">10</reference>). Even the heathen believed that breakers of an oath would not "escape" punishment. <div eID="gen20377" type="x-p"/>
entries.7a1ce7940158c2930f56e1eb6ce2a4cca2b2255e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11277"/><div sID="gen20378" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11277"/><hi type="bold">16. in the place where the king dwelleth--</hi>righteous retribution. He brought on himself in the worst form the evil which, in a mild form, he had sought to deliver himself from by perjured treachery, namely, vassalage (<reference osisRef="Ezek.12.13">Eze 12:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.32.5">Jr 32:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.34.3">34:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.52.11">52:11</reference>). <div eID="gen20378" type="x-p"/>
entries.45b25f8574ab481728763e3327a20e6bf252a596: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11278"/><div sID="gen20379" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11278"/><hi type="bold">17. Pharaoh--</hi>Pharaoh-hophra (<reference osisRef="Jer.37.7">Jr 37:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.44.30">44:30</reference>), the successor of Necho (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.29">2Ki 23:29</reference>).<div eID="gen20379" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20380" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Neither ... make for him--</hi>literally, "effect (anything) with him," that is, be of any avail to Zedekiah. Pharaoh did not act in concert with him, for he was himself compelled to retire to Egypt.<div eID="gen20380" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20381" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">by casting up mounts, &c.--</hi>So far from Pharaoh doing so for Jerusalem, this was what Nebuchadnezzar did against it (<reference osisRef="Jer.52.4">Jr 52:4</reference>). Calvin Maurer, &c., refer it to Nebuchadnezzar, "when Nebuchadnezzar shall cast up mounts." <div eID="gen20381" type="x-p"/>
entries.19069813b66a1517744e651f2225006c495ff570: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11279"/><div sID="gen20382" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11279"/><hi type="bold">18. given his hand--</hi>in ratification of the oath (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.10.15">2Ki 10:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezra.10.19">Ezr 10:19</reference>), and also in token of subjection to Nebuchadnezzar (<reference osisRef="1Chr.29.24">1Ch 29:24</reference>, Margin; <reference osisRef="2Chr.30.8">2Ch 30:8</reference>, Margin; <reference osisRef="Lam.5.6">La 5:6</reference>). <div eID="gen20382" type="x-p"/>
entries.547a7c0b965a5422bfad966a586e1d9dd408e57f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11280"/><div sID="gen20383" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11280"/><hi type="bold">19. mine oath--</hi>The "covenant" being sworn in God's name was really His covenant; a new instance in relation to man of the treacherous spirit which had been so often betrayed in relation to God. God Himself must therefore avenge the violation of His covenant "on the head" of the perjurer (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.7.16">Psa 7:16</reference>). <div eID="gen20383" type="x-p"/>
entries.0e7af4a0d1d83f68dc74bd9fc77d906d965a6f8b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11281"/><div sID="gen20384" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11281"/><hi type="bold">20. my net--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ezek.12.13">Eze 12:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.32.3">32:3</reference>). God entraps him as he had tried to entrap others (<reference osisRef="Ps.7.15">Psa 7:15</reference>). This was spoken at least upwards of three years before the fall of Jerusalem (compare <reference osisRef="Ezek.8.1">Eze 8:1</reference>, with <reference osisRef="Ezek.20.1">Eze 20:1</reference>).<div eID="gen20384" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20385" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">plead with him--</hi>by judgments on him (Eze 20. 36). <div eID="gen20385" type="x-p"/>
entries.6679feed0c3e5e557a7ac7dbb06a3e296e33118d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11282"/><div sID="gen20386" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11282"/><hi type="bold">21. all his fugitives--</hi>the soldiers that accompany him in his flight. <div eID="gen20386" type="x-p"/>
entries.804159b238ed64e71c84902371dcf25f3e7b751b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11283"/><div sID="gen20387" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11283"/>22. When the state of Israel shall seem past recovery, Messiah, Jehovah Himself, will unexpectedly appear on the scene as Redeemer of His people (<reference osisRef="Isa.63.5">Is 63:5</reference>).<div eID="gen20387" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20388" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I ... also--</hi>God opposes Himself to Nebuchadnezzar: "He took of the seed of the land and planted it (<reference osisRef="Ezek.17.3">Eze 17:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.17.5">5</reference>), so will I, but with better success than he had. The branch he plucked (Zedekiah) and planted, flourished but for a time, to perish at last; I will plant a scion of the same tree, the house of David, to whom the kingdom belongs by an everlasting covenant, and it shall be the shelter of the whole world, and shall be for ever."<div eID="gen20388" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20389" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">branch--</hi>the peculiar title of Messiah (<reference osisRef="Zech.3.8">Zec 3:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.6.12">6:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.11.1">Is 11:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.4.2">4:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.23.5">Jr 23:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.33.15">33:15</reference>).<div eID="gen20389" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20390" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">a tender one--</hi>Zerubbabel never reigned as a universal (<reference osisRef="Ezek.17.23">Eze 17:23</reference>) king, nor could the great things mentioned here be said of him, except as a type of Messiah. Messiah alone can be meant: originally "a tender plant and root out of a dry ground" (<reference osisRef="Isa.53.2">Is 53:2</reference>); the beginning of His kingdom being humble, His reputed parents of lowly rank, though King David's lineal representatives; yet, even then, God here calls Him, in respect to His everlasting purpose, "the highest ... of the high" (<reference osisRef="Ps.89.27">Psa 89:27</reference>).<div eID="gen20390" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20391" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I ... will plant it upon an high mountain--</hi>Zion; destined to be the moral center and eminence of grace and glory shining forth to the world, out-topping all mundane elevation. The kingdom, typically begun at the return from Babylon, and the rebuilding of the temple, fully began with Christ's appearing, and shall have its highest manifestation at His reappearing to reign on Zion, and thence over the whole earth (<reference osisRef="Ps.2.6">Psa 2:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.8">8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.2.2">Is 2:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.3">3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.3.17">Jr 3:17</reference>). <div eID="gen20391" type="x-p"/>
entries.cacf24b8c63b6a3a691996715a0b7a4108ef7da9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11284"/><div sID="gen20392" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11284"/><hi type="bold">23. under it ... all fowl--</hi>the Gospel "mustard tree," small at first, but at length receiving all under its covert (<reference osisRef="Matt.13.32">Mt 13:32</reference>); the antithesis to Antichrist, symbolized by Assyria, of which the same is said (<reference osisRef="Ezek.31.6">Eze 31:6</reference>), and Babylon (<reference osisRef="Dan.4.12">Da 4:12</reference>). Antichrist assumes in mimicry the universal power really belonging to Christ. <div eID="gen20392" type="x-p"/>
entries.e0eaa86fcdd1681ba34d9ff210a7d3d654643893: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11285"/><div sID="gen20393" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11285"/><hi type="bold">24. I ... brought down the high--</hi>the very attribute given to God by the virgin mother of Him, under whom this was to be accomplished.<div eID="gen20393" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20394" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">high ... low tree--</hi>that is, princes elevated ... depressed. All the empires of the world, represented by Babylon, once flourishing ("green"), shall be brought low before the once depressed ("dry"), but then exalted, kingdom of Messiah and His people, the head of whom shall be Israel (<reference osisRef="Dan.2.44">Da 2:44</reference>). <chapter eID="Ezek.17"/>

entries.8f4e1ab058c551a629dcd316a17528344cd9cb42: <div eID="gen31605" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen31606" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen31607" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen31607" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen31606" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen31608" type="x-p"/> This chapter begins with a new allegory or parable, <reference osisRef="Eze.17.1-Eze.17.10">Eze 17:1-10</reference>; to which an explanation is immediately subjoined, <reference osisRef="Eze.17.11-Eze.17.21">Eze 17:11-21</reference>. In the remaining verses the prophet, by a beautiful metaphor, makes an easy and natural transition to the Messiah, and predicts the security, increasing prosperity, and ultimate universality of his kingdom, <reference osisRef="Eze.17.22-Eze.17.24">Eze 17:22-24</reference>. From the beauty of its images, the elegance of its composition, the perspicuity of its language, the rich variety of its matter, and the easy transition from one part of the subject to another, this chapter forms one of the most beautiful and perfect pieces of its kind that can possibly be conceived in so small a compass; and then the unexpected change from objects that presented nothing to the view but gloom and horror, to a prospect of ineffable glory and beauty, has a most happy effect. Every lowering cloud is dispelled, and the fields again smile in the beams of midday. The traveler, who this moment trembled as he looked around for shelter, now proceeds on has way rejoicing.
entries.e968cde2eeee3998f9c9e351ca8162c9db0db61a: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen31608" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31609" type="x-p"/> Son of man, put forth a riddle - Riddle, Anglo-Saxon, from to divine; a thing that must be curiously investigated and sifted, to find out the meaning; and hence, riddle, a sort of coarse sieve to clean corn, to separate coarse chaff and straws from the pure grain. An instrument formerly used for divination. This is not far removed from the Hebrew חידה chidah, from חד chad, to penetrate; not that which penetrates the mind, but which we must penetrate to find out the sense.
entries.db90d87554be06194dc5640dedc0f3f40c7977c5: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen31609" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31610" type="x-p"/> A great eagle - Nebuchadnezzar. See <reference osisRef="Jer.48.40">Jer 48:40</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.49.22">Jer 49:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.7.4">Dan 7:4</reference>. And see here, <reference osisRef="Dan.7.12">Dan 7:12</reference>, where it is so applied. <div eID="gen31610" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31611" type="x-p"/> Great wings - Extensive empire. <div eID="gen31611" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31612" type="x-p"/> Long-winged - Rapid in his conquests. <div eID="gen31612" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31613" type="x-p"/> Full of feathers - Having multitudes of subjects. <div eID="gen31613" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31614" type="x-p"/> Divers colors - People of various nations. <div eID="gen31614" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31615" type="x-p"/> Came unto Lebanon - Came against Judea. <div eID="gen31615" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31616" type="x-p"/> The highest branch - King Jehoiachin he took captive to Babylon. <div eID="gen31616" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31617" type="x-p"/> The cedar - The Jewish state and king.
entries.ca12b2210bb4a1ef3965086e8de4dd157849978f: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen31617" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31618" type="x-p"/> The top of his young twigs - The princes of Judah. <div eID="gen31618" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31619" type="x-p"/> A land of traffic - Chaldea. <div eID="gen31619" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31620" type="x-p"/> A city of merchants - Babylon; for which this city was the most celebrated of all the cities of the east. Its situation procured it innumerable advantages; its two rivers, the Tigris and Euphrates, and the Persian Gulf, gave it communication with the richest and the most distant nations.
entries.e7c08e3d9011749b0c3455e7f21d12e0aa2ddb9e: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen31620" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31621" type="x-p"/> The seed of the land - Zedekiah, brother of Jehoiachin. <div eID="gen31621" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31622" type="x-p"/> Planted it in a fruitful field - Made him king of Judea in place of his brother. <div eID="gen31622" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31623" type="x-p"/> Placed it by great waters - Put him under the protection of Babylon, situated on the confluence of the Tigris and Euphrates. <div eID="gen31623" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31624" type="x-p"/> And set it as a willow tree - Made him dependent on this city of great waters, as the willow is on humidity.
entries.b613f5dcfef4adbd1a6fe3030d7b5317de490dbe: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen31624" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31625" type="x-p"/> A spreading vine of low stature - The Jewish state having then no height of dominion, it must abide under the wings or branches of the Chaldean king. <div eID="gen31625" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31626" type="x-p"/> Those branches turned toward him, and the roots - under him - Zedekiah was wholly dependent on Nebuchadnezzar, both for his elevation to the throne, and his support on it.
entries.96560f870aff92710bdc1d830e1b8ec8c09af906: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen31626" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31627" type="x-p"/> Another great eagle - Pharaoh-hophra, or Apries, king of Egypt. <div eID="gen31627" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31628" type="x-p"/> With great wings - Extensive dominion. <div eID="gen31628" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31629" type="x-p"/> And many feathers - Numerous subjects. <div eID="gen31629" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31630" type="x-p"/> Did bend her roots - Looked to him for support in her intended rebellion against Nebuchadnezzar.
entries.cd67e5e7b0b72f94897fcae3f1ae92bb5870ba8d: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen31630" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31631" type="x-p"/> It was planted in a good soil - Though he depended on Babylon, he lived and reigned as Nebuchadnezzar's vicegerent in the land of Judea.
entries.ed091d489a307d570276c42b671ffd393293ef0d: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen31631" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31632" type="x-p"/> Shall it prosper? - Shall Zedekiah succeed in casting off the yoke of the king of Babylon, to whom he had sworn fealty? <div eID="gen31632" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31633" type="x-p"/> Shall he not pull up the roots - Nebuchadnezzar will come and dethrone him. <div eID="gen31633" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31634" type="x-p"/> And cut off the fruit - The children of Zedekiah. <div eID="gen31634" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31635" type="x-p"/> The leaves - All the nobles; all shall perish with Zedekiah.
entries.e33497d4f4e29ce7f0b93497a237cfb83718024a: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen31635" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31636" type="x-p"/> Shall - utterly whither - The regal government shall be no more restored. Zedekiah shall be the last king, and the monarchy shall finally terminate with him.
entries.4a782e037f5f5b7528294b067cbd76a0bf030c4d: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen31636" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31637" type="x-p"/> Know ye not what these things mean? - They are explained in this and the following verses.
entries.13e6727b47ea0b6488371ded120ad4811d3773fb: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen31637" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31638" type="x-p"/> That the kingdom might be base - Have no political consequence, and at last sink into a miserable government under Gedaliah.
entries.82024d1df2b1e58dcaf0c40631110b66b149dbb7: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen31638" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31639" type="x-p"/> Sending his ambassadors into Egypt - Zedekiah must have sent his ambassadors into Egypt, between the sixth month of his sixth year, and the fifth month of his seventh year. Compare <reference osisRef="Eze.8.1">Eze 8:1</reference>, with <reference osisRef="Eze.20.1">Eze 20:1</reference>. - See Newcome.
entries.e7693c125f11abe66fe1dd19b557f232136db36f: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen31639" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31640" type="x-p"/> In the midst of Babylon he shall die - His eyes were put out; he was carried to Babylon, and never returned.
entries.8389e3752defa53eee08096c9ceb85abeea831a6: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen31640" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31641" type="x-p"/> Seeing he despised the oath - This God particularly resents. He had bound himself by oath, in the presence of Jehovah, to be faithful to the covenant that he made with Nebuchadnezzar, and he took the first opportunity to break it; therefore he shall not escape.
entries.3ebab8eaf06d4f001800a5dce268b647178ebe55: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen31641" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31642" type="x-p"/> I will spread my net upon him - See the note on <reference osisRef="Eze.12.13">Eze 12:13</reference>.
entries.901f207d7126da225294d142b1f29e7c890ebcdd: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen31642" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31643" type="x-p"/> All his fugitives - All who attempted to escape with him, and all that ran to Egypt, etc., shall fall by the sword.
entries.fa3b8aab057c44a2563737e05ad15932560de8f4: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen31643" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31644" type="x-p"/> I will also take of the highest branch of the high cedar - I will raise up another monarchy, which shall come in the line of David, namely, the Messiah; who shall appear as a tender plant, as to his incarnation; but he shall be high and eminent; his Church, the royal city, the highest and purest ever seen on the face of the earth.
entries.abdc41ad4c565052016cfb44e16def88ddcd512a: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen31644" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31645" type="x-p"/> In the mountain of the height of Israel - He shall make his appearance at the temple, and found his Church at Jerusalem. <div eID="gen31645" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31646" type="x-p"/> Shalt bring forth boughs - Apostles, evangelists, and their successors in the Gospel ministry. <div eID="gen31646" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31647" type="x-p"/> And bear fruit - Multitudes of souls shall be converted by their preaching. <div eID="gen31647" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31648" type="x-p"/> And under it shall dwell all fowl of every wing - All the nations of the earth shall receive his Gospel. <div eID="gen31648" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31649" type="x-p"/> In the shadow of the branches thereof shall they dwell - Trust in him alone for salvation, and be saved in their trusting.
entries.2acd5a288e389b6f007b04b4dd3acd2180bd5294: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen31649" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31650" type="x-p"/> All the trees of the field shall know - All the people of Israel and of Chaldea. <div eID="gen31650" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31651" type="x-p"/> I the Lord have brought down the high tree - Have dethroned Jehoiachin. <div eID="gen31651" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31652" type="x-p"/> Have exalted the low tree - Put Zedekiah, brother of Jehoiachin, in his place. <div eID="gen31652" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31653" type="x-p"/> Have dried up the green tree - Zedekiah, who had numerous children, but who were all slain before his eyes at Riblah. <div eID="gen31653" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31654" type="x-p"/> And have made the dry tree to flourish - Have raised up a rod out of the stem of Jesse, the family of David being then apparently dried up and extinct. This was the promised Messiah, of the increase and government of whose kingdom and peace there shall be no end; upon the throne of David, and upon his kingdom, to order and establish it with judgment and with justice, from henceforth, even for ever. The Zeal of The Lord of Hosts Will Perform This. <div eID="gen31654" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31655" type="x-p"/> The high and green tree, says Newcome, refers to Nebuchadnezzar; the low and the dry tree, to the Jews.  <chapter eID="Ezek.17"/> <div eID="gen31655" type="x-p"/>

entries.806dee194947324ef86a02820d0c8c49b0e44c70: <div eID="gen14929" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">Humiliation and Exaltation of the Davidic Family</title> <div sID="gen14930" type="x-p"/> The contents of this chapter are introduced as a riddle and a parable, and are divided into three sections. <reference osisRef="Ezek.17.1-Ezek.17.10">Eze 17:1-10</reference> contain the parable; <reference osisRef="Ezek.17.11-Ezek.17.21">Eze 17:11-21</reference>, the interpretation and application of it to King Zedekiah; and <reference osisRef="Ezek.17.22-Ezek.17.24">Eze 17:22-24</reference>, the promise of the Messianic kingdom. <div eID="gen14930" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14931" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Ezek.17.1-Ezek.17.10">Eze 17:1-10</reference> <div eID="gen14931" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">The Parable</title> <div sID="gen14932" type="x-p"/> Eze 17:1. <hi type="italic">And the word of Jehovah came to me, saying,</hi> Eze 17:2. <hi type="italic">Son of man, give a riddle, and relate a parable to the house of Israel;</hi> Eze 17:3. <hi type="italic">And say, Thus saith the Lord Jehovah, A great eagle, with great wings and long pinions, full of feathers of variegated colours, came to Lebanon and took the top of the cedar:</hi> Eze 17:4. <hi type="italic">He plucked off the topmost of its shoots, and brought it into Canaan’s land; in a merchant-city he set it.</hi> Eze 17:5. <hi type="italic">And he took of the seed of the land, and put it into seed-land; took it away to many waters, set it as a willow.</hi> Eze 17:6. <hi type="italic">And it grew, and became an overhanging vine of low stature, that its branches might turn towards him, and its roots might be under him; and it became a vine, and produced shoots, and sent out foliage.</hi> Eze 17:7. <hi type="italic">There was another great eagle with great wings and many feathers; and, behold, this vine stretched its roots languishingly towards him, and extended its branches towards him, that he might water it from the beds of its planting.</hi> Eze 17:8. <hi type="italic">It was planted in a good field by many waters, to send out roots and bear fruit, to become a glorious vine.</hi> Eze 17:9. <hi type="italic">Say, Thus saith the Lord Jehovah, Will it thrive? will they not pull up its roots, and cut off its fruit, so that it withereth? all the fresh leaves of its sprouting will wither, and not with strong arm and with much people will it be possible to raise it up from its roots.</hi> Eze 17:10. <hi type="italic">And, behold, although it is planted, will it thrive? will it not wither when the east wind touches it? upon the beds in which it grew it will wither.</hi> <div eID="gen14932" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14933" type="x-p"/> The parable (<hi type="italic">mâshâl</hi>, corresponding exactly to the New Testament παραβολή) is called <hi type="italic">chīdhâh</hi>, a riddle, because of the deeper meaning lying beneath the parabolic shell. The symbolism of this parable has been traced by many commentators to Babylonian influences working upon the prophet’s mind; but without any tenable ground. The figure of the eagle, or bird of prey, applied to a conqueror making a rapid descent upon a country, has as little in it of a specifically Babylonian character as the comparison of the royal family to a cedar or a vine. Not only is Nebuchadnezzar compared to an eagle in <reference osisRef="Jer.48.40">Jer 48:40</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.49.22">Jer 49:22</reference>, as Cyrus is to a bird of prey in <reference osisRef="Isa.46.11">Isa 46:11</reference>; but even Moses has described the paternal watchfulness of God over His own people as bearing them upon eagle’s wings (<reference osisRef="Exod.19.4">Exo 19:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.32.11">Deu 32:11</reference>). The cedar of Lebanon and the vine are genuine Israelitish figures. The great eagle in <reference osisRef="Ezek.17.3">Eze 17:3</reference> is the great King Nebuchadnezzar (compare <reference osisRef="Ezek.17.12">Eze 17:12</reference>). The article is simply used to indicate the species, for which we should use the indefinite article. In <reference osisRef="Ezek.17.7">Eze 17:7</reference>, instead of the article, we have אחד in the sense of “another.” This first eagle has large wings and long pinions; he has already flown victoriously over wide-spread countries. אשׁר־לו , literally, which is to him the variegated ornament, i.e., which he has as such an ornament. The feathers of variegated ornamental colours point to the many peoples, differing in language, manners, and customs, which were united under the sceptre of Nebuchadnezzar (Hitzig, etc.); not to the wealth and splendour of the conqueror, as such an allusion is altogether remote from the tendency of the parable. He came to Lebanon.
